newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dollar may test below 118 yen in Asia.
newsitem.headline: Dollar may test below 118 yen in Asia.

text.p: The dollar is expected to be vulnerable and heading lower during Asian trading time on Wednesday, with a re-test of the 117-118 yen level possible although a fall to the recent 117.50 yen low is unlikely.
Weaker U.S. April retail sales figures, released Tuesday, raised questions about the chance of a U.S. interest rate rise next week and sparked dollar sales overnight.

The mark's weakness against the yen also weighed on the dollar against the yen, and was expected to lead trade during Asian time, dealers said, with falls to near 69.50 yen possible after heavy offers emerged near 70.20-30 yen overnight.

The greenback was already under selling pressure during early Asian trade as stop-loss sales were set off at 118.40 yen. The mark slipped from 70.03 yen at the New York close to around 69.77/80 yen as of 2300 GMT, mainly on sales from overseas operators, a trust bank dealer said.

The Commerce Department said total retail sales fell 0.3 percent in April, the largest drop since a 0.5 percent decline last June. Excluding autos, sales slid 0.1 percent in April instead of rising 0.1 percent as expected in a Reuter poll.
Dealers said these figures may add fuel to market speculation that the Fed will not raise U.S. rates next week.
Some buying of the greenback at its lows was detected Tuesday from institutional investors, probably life insurers, and dealers said one focus of today's trade will be if such buying emerges again.
"If not, we could well see the dollar head sharply lower, especially as some loss-cut selling may develop should the dollar break below 117 yen," a city bank dealer said.

While short-covering may help prop the dollar temporarily, this is not expected to be active, he added, with the topside growing gradually heavier. U.S. funds may bid for the dollar, but then are likely to sell for profits at the highs.

The market will watch for comments from Japanese officials as well as the release at 2350 GMT of Japan's March current account data. A drop in the surplus is expected, but economists have said that this is likely to be the last drop for some time, with sharp rises forecast for April, May and June.
The surplus in the current account -- the broadest measure of trade in goods and services -- has been the focus of recent trade tension with the United States.
